timetran.title: Timestamp Converter
timetran.desc: Convert between Unix timestamps and human-readable dates.
timetran.what_is_content: Unix Timestamp is the number of seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970 00:00:00 UTC, not counting leap seconds. It is widely used in computer systems for its cross-platform and cross-timezone advantages.
timetran.why_need_content: While timestamps are computer-friendly, they are hard for humans to read (e.g., 1704067200 is 2024-01-01). Developers often need to convert between 'readable dates' and 'timestamps' when debugging, analyzing logs, or handling database data.
timetran.q1: Q: What is the Year 2038 problem?
timetran.a1: A: In systems using 32-bit signed integers, the max timestamp is 2147483647 (Jan 19, 2038). Beyond this, it overflows. 64-bit systems solve this.
timetran.a2: A: Usually seconds are 10 digits, milliseconds are 13. This tool auto-detects length.
timetran.a3: A: UTC is the world standard. Local time includes your timezone offset (e.g., UTC+8). Timestamps are based on UTC.

md5.title: MD5 Encryption
md5.what_is_content: MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5) is a widely used cryptographic hash function producing a 128-bit (16-byte) hash value, typically expressed as a 32-digit hexadecimal number. Designed by Ron Rivest in 1991 to ensure data integrity.
md5.use_check: Integrity Check: Verifying file integrity by comparing MD5 checksums.
md5.use_sign: Digital Signature: Ensuring messages are not modified during transmission.
md5.use_store: Secure Storage (Obsolete): Formerly used for password hashing, now discouraged due to collision vulnerabilities.
md5.warning_content:
MD5 is no longer considered secure against collision attacks. Generating collisions or using rainbow tables to reverse hashes is feasible with modern hardware.

Guidelines:
1. Do NOT use MD5 for password storage. Use bcrypt, Argon2 or PBKDF2.
2. Do NOT use MD5 for high-security digital signatures. Use SHA-256 or SHA-3.
md5.a1: A: MD5 always produces 128 bits (32 hex chars). '16-bit MD5' is just a substring of the middle 16 characters (removing first/last 8). They represent the same hash.
md5.a2: A: Theoretically, MD5 is a one-way hash function and cannot be 'decrypted'. However, using 'Rainbow Tables' (massive databases of precomputed hashes), one can find the original string for many common inputs.

httpstatus.title: HTTP Status Codes
httpstatus.desc: Comprehensive list of HTTP status codes with detailed explanations
httpstatus.group_2xx: 2xx Success - The action was successfully received, understood, and accepted
httpstatus.group_3xx: 3xx Redirection - Further action must be taken in order to complete the request
httpstatus.group_4xx: 4xx Client Error - The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled
httpstatus.group_5xx: 5xx Server Error - The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request

100.name: Continue
100.desc: The server has received the request headers and the client should proceed to send the request body.

101.name: Switching Protocols
101.desc: The requester has asked the server to switch protocols and the server has agreed to do so.

102.name: Processing
102.desc: A WebDAV request may contain many sub-requests involving file operations, requiring a long time to complete the request.

200.name: OK
200.desc: Standard response for successful HTTP requests.

201.name: Created
201.desc: The request has been fulfilled, resulting in the creation of a new resource.

202.name: Accepted
202.desc: The request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed.

203.name: Non-Authoritative Information
203.desc: The server is a transforming proxy that received a 200 OK from its upstream, but is returning a modified version of the upstream's response.

204.name: No Content
204.desc: The server successfully processed the request and is not returning any content.

205.name: Reset Content
205.desc: The server successfully processed the request, but is not returning any content and requires that the requester reset the document view.

206.name: Partial Content
206.desc: The server is delivering only part of the resource (byte serving) due to a range header sent by the client.

207.name: Multi-Status
207.desc: The message body that follows is by default an XML message and can contain a number of separate response codes, depending on how many sub-requests were made.

208.name: Already Reported
208.desc: The members of a DAV binding have already been enumerated in a preceding part of the (multistatus) response, and are not being included again.

226.name: IM Used
226.desc: The server has fulfilled a request for the resource, and the response is a representation of the result of one or more instance-manipulations applied to the current instance.

300.name: Multiple Choices
300.desc: Indicates multiple options for the resource from which the client may choose.

301.name: Moved Permanently
301.desc: This and all future requests should be directed to the given URI.

302.name: Found
302.desc: Tells the client to look at (browse to) another URL. 302 has been superseded by 303 and 307.

303.name: See Other
303.desc: The response to the request can be found under another URI using a GET method.

304.name: Not Modified
304.desc: Indicates that the resource has not been modified since the version specified by the request headers.

305.name: Use Proxy
305.desc: The requested resource is available only through a proxy, the address for which is provided in the response.

306.name: Switch Proxy
306.desc: No longer used. Originally meant 'Subsequent requests should use the specified proxy'.

307.name: Temporary Redirect
307.desc: In this case, the request should be repeated with another URI; however, future requests should still use the original URI.

308.name: Permanent Redirect
308.desc: The request and all future requests should be repeated using another URI.

400.name: Bad Request
400.desc: The server cannot or will not process the request due to an apparent client error.

401.name: Unauthorized
401.desc: Similar to 403 Forbidden, but specifically for use when authentication is required and has failed or has not yet been provided.

402.name: Payment Required
402.desc: Reserved for future use. The original intention was that this code might be used as part of some form of digital cash or micropayment scheme.

403.name: Forbidden
403.desc: The request was valid, but the server is refusing action. The user might not have the necessary permissions for a resource.

404.name: Not Found
404.desc: The requested resource could not be found but may be available in the future. Subsequent requests by the client are permissible.

405.name: Method Not Allowed
405.desc: A request method is not supported for the requested resource.

406.name: Not Acceptable
406.desc: The requested resource is capable of generating only content not acceptable according to the Accept headers sent in the request.

407.name: Proxy Authentication Required
407.desc: The client must first authenticate itself with the proxy.

408.name: Request Timeout
408.desc: The server timed out waiting for the request.

409.name: Conflict
409.desc: Indicates that the request could not be processed because of conflict in the request.

410.name: Gone
410.desc: Indicates that the resource requested is no longer available and will not be available again.

411.name: Length Required
411.desc: The request did not specify the length of its content, which is required by the requested resource.

412.name: Precondition Failed
412.desc: The server does not meet one of the preconditions that the requester put on the request.

413.name: Payload Too Large
413.desc: The request is larger than the server is willing or able to process.

414.name: URI Too Long
414.desc: The URI provided was too long for the server to process.

415.name: Unsupported Media Type
415.desc: The request entity has a media type which the server or resource does not support.

416.name: Range Not Satisfiable
416.desc: The client has asked for a portion of the file (byte serving), but the server cannot supply that portion.

417.name: Expectation Failed
417.desc: The server cannot meet the requirements of the Expect request-header field.

418.name: I'm a teapot
418.desc: This code was defined in 1998 as one of the traditional IETF April Fools' jokes, in RFC 2324, Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, and is not expected to be implemented by actual HTTP servers.

421.name: Misdirected Request
421.desc: The request was directed at a server that is not able to produce a response.

422.name: Unprocessable Entity
422.desc: The request was well-formed but was unable to be followed due to semantic errors.

423.name: Locked
423.desc: The resource that is being accessed is locked.

424.name: Failed Dependency
424.desc: The request failed due to failure of a previous request.

425.name: Too Early
425.desc: Indicates that the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed.

426.name: Upgrade Required
426.desc: The client should switch to a different protocol such as TLS/1.0, given in the Upgrade header field.

429.name: Too Many Requests
429.desc: The user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. Intended for use with rate-limiting schemes.

431.name: Request Header Fields Too Large
431.desc: The server is unwilling to process the request because either an individual header field, or all the header fields collectively, are too large.

449.name: Retry With
449.desc: A Microsoft extension. The request should be retried after performing the appropriate action.

451.name: Unavailable For Legal Reasons
451.desc: A server operator has received a legal demand to deny access to a resource or to a set of resources that includes the requested resource.

500.name: Internal Server Error
500.desc: A generic error message, given when an unexpected condition was encountered and no more specific message is suitable.

501.name: Not Implemented
501.desc: The server either does not recognize the request method, or it lacks the ability to fulfill the request.

502.name: Bad Gateway
502.desc: The server was acting as a gateway or proxy and received an invalid response from the upstream server.

503.name: Service Unavailable
503.desc: The server is currently unavailable (because it is overloaded or down for maintenance). Generally, this is a temporary state.

504.name: Gateway Timeout
504.desc: The server was acting as a gateway or proxy and did not receive a timely response from the upstream server.

505.name: HTTP Version Not Supported
505.desc: The server does not support the HTTP protocol version used in the request.

506.name: Variant Also Negotiates
506.desc: Transparent content negotiation for the request results in a circular reference.

507.name: Insufficient Storage
507.desc: The server is unable to store the representation needed to complete the request.

508.name: Loop Detected
508.desc: The server detected an infinite loop while processing the request.

510.name: Not Extended
510.desc: Further extensions to the request are required for the server to fulfill it.

511.name: Network Authentication Required
511.desc: The client needs to authenticate to gain network access.

colorpicker.title: Color Picker
colorpicker.desc_intro:
Convert colors between different formats (Hex, RGB, HSL, CSS names)

In CSS, color is everywhere, it can be used for text, background, shadow, border, link, etc. Most colors we use in CSS are Hex and RGB, but there are many ways to represent color;
colorpicker.desc_rgb: - RGB: RGB values are also commonly used color representations. RGB stands for Red-Green-Blue, the order is very important. Each color is specified by a number between 0 and 255. Most common RGB values are Black: rgb(0,0,0) and White: rgb(255,255,255). RGB notation gives us access to the same range of colors as Hex values in a more readable form.
colorpicker.desc_hex: - Hex: You can use hexadecimal values to represent colors in CSS, which is the most used way. Hexadecimal uses 16 symbols, 0-9 represent values 0-9, A-F represent values 10-15
colorpicker.desc_hsl: - HSL: HSL stands for Hue-Saturation-Lightness. It is based on the RGB color wheel. Each color has an angle and percentage values for saturation and lightness
colorpicker.desc_hsv: - HSV: HSV color space is an improvement on the traditional RGB model, introducing three main components to define color: Hue (H), Saturation (S), and Value (V). Unlike RGB, it provides a more intuitive way to describe color based on dominant wavelength, saturation, and brightness.
colorpicker.desc_lab: - LAB: LAB is a color space accessible in software like Photoshop, representing the entire range of colors visible to humans. It uses three axes: Lightness, a-axis, and b-axis.
colorpicker.desc_lch: - LCH: LCH stands for Lightness, Chroma, and Hue. It has the same L value as Lab, but instead of coordinates a* and b*, it uses C (Chroma) and H (Hue). Hue can be a value between 0 and 360. Chroma represents the amount of color, similar to Saturation in HSL, but Chroma values can exceed 100, theoretically limitless.
colorpicker.desc_cmyk: - CMYK: CMYK stands for Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, and Key, matching ink colors in printers. While screens display colors in RGB, printers use a combination of Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, and Black inks.
